question: Is death final?
summary: The Hebrew Bible's wisdom literature and older narrative strata treat death as terminal — the dead go to Sheol, lose consciousness, and do not return. Later texts (Daniel 12, Isaiah 26:19) and the New Testament insist on bodily resurrection and conscious afterlife. The two views can't both describe the same anthropology — they reflect different stages in the development of Israelite and early Jewish thought about the dead.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read the wisdom literature's terminal-death language as describing only the loss of bodily, earthly life, not the soul's continued existence — so the OT texts and the resurrection hope can both stand.

discrepancy.connective: Robert Martin-Achard argued that early Israel knew no resurrection: Sheol was a shadowy non-life from which none returned, and the conscious afterlife and bodily resurrection of Daniel, Isaiah 26, and the New Testament are a late development that broke with the older view.

skeptic.name: Robert Martin-Achard
skeptic.work: From Death to Life: A Study of the Development of the Doctrine of the Resurrection in the Old Testament

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Ecclesiastes 9:5; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:5; Psalm 115:17
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage cluster directly, repeatedly arguing that the wisdom literature's death-is-final language denies only bodily, earthly existence (not the soul's survival) and is compatible with conscious afterlife and resurrection. Haley's coverage of this specific death-finality discrepancy could not be confirmed, so a harmonizing commentator surfaced on this row is used.

link.title: GotQuestions: What does it mean that the dead know nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5)?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the most-cited proof text, harmonizing Eccl 9:5 with a conscious afterlife via the 'under the sun' earthly-perspective reading.

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: but the dead know not anything; this is not to be understood of their separate spirits, and of the things of the other world; for the righteous dead know much, their knowledge is greatly increased … but this is to be interpreted of their bodily senses now extinct, and of worldly things they have now nothing to do with; they know not any thing that is done in this world …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Eccl 9:5 ('the dead know not anything') is the single most-cited proof that the OT treats death as terminal/unconscious. Gill harmonizes the most contested verse directly, restricting its denial to bodily senses and worldly affairs while affirming the soul's continued, even increased, knowledge — the strongest both-true reading of this passage cluster.
